title: Alice Lai - All Together Now: Creating Multiplicative Power in Hades
speaker: Alice Lai
summary: Supergiant technical designer Alice Lai discusses combos ('multiplicative power') in action roguelikes, using Binding of Isaac and Enter the Gungeon as examples before turning to Hades. She argues combos are content, a source of mastery, and a way for players to shape their own difficulty curve. In Hades, combos are kept legible by giving each reward system (Hermes/Mirror, hammers/aspects, gods/duo boons) a clear, bounded role, and kept special by capping how many upgrades of each kind a run offers. She also covers the JSON-driven trait system, order-dependence bugs, thematic god-driven content brainstorming, and the house-of-cards entropy of late development.

insights.claim: In The Binding of Isaac, three individually mediocre items (Swallowed Penny, Bloody Penny, Money = Power) combine into an engine of near-infinite coins, health and damage.
insights.detail: Alone, coins on damage, health on coin pickup and damage scaling with money are each only modest. Combined, with a blood donation machine, they let the player max out money and damage at once. Lai presents this as a combo whose synergy players can intuit from the item effects.
insights.quote: if you combine all of these together uh you kind of create this great engine if you find a blood donation machine to just get infinite coins and infinite health

insights.claim: Enter the Gungeon signals hidden, back-end combos through shared theming, so players infer that thematically related items (e.g. bee items) will synergize.
insights.detail: Unlike Isaac's mechanically intuitable combos, Gungeon's combos are scripted on the back end and the only hint to the player is similar theming. Players then learn the pattern that collecting bee-related items yields bee combos.
insights.quote: for the player the only thing that implies it is that they have the similar theming uh they are all bee-related items

insights.claim: Combos, defined as two or more elements producing a new and unexpected result, should be counted as game content alongside areas, monsters and biomes.
insights.detail: Lai argues that when designers think of content they list areas, spells, monsters and biomes, but emergent combo interactions are a big part of a game's content too, and learning them builds a sense of mastery.
insights.quote: combos are anything anytime when two or more elements provide a new and unexpected result

insights.claim: Known combos let players deliberately shape their own power and difficulty curve within a run, which produces a feeling of mastery.
insights.detail: A player who knows a combo can choose to chase or avoid it, and can trade off: take an early combo to breeze through two areas but struggle later, or suffer early and pick up the combo enabler in the last area to leap ahead of the difficulty curve.
insights.quote: it also allows players to influence the power and difficulty curve in ways that let them feel a lot of mastery as well

insights.claim: Hades' gun secondary build stacks Cluster Bomb (five grenades), Rocket Bomb (rockets) and Dionysus' Flourish (stacking damage over time) into a rocket shotgun that applies DoT far faster than normal.
insights.detail: Each ability modifies the same secondary attack, and together they produce a damage-over-time application rate at levels the player normally could not reach.
insights.quote: you kind of get this like rocket launching uh rocket shotgun ability that allows you to apply this damage over time effect really quickly

insights.claim: Hades builds upgrades that either remove a base ability's downside or amplify its upside, as with Ares' Blade Rift plus Engulfing Vortex and Vicious Cycle.
insights.detail: The Blade Rift cast deals heavy damage but is slow and easy for enemies to walk out of. Engulfing Vortex pulls enemies in (removing the downside) and Vicious Cycle increases damage the longer enemies stay inside (amplifying the upside), each changing how the player interacts with the ability.
insights.quote: it takes an ability and either removes its downsides or extenuates upsides

insights.claim: Hades gives each upgrade system a clearly bounded goal (Hermes/Mirror make you plainly better, hammers/aspects change weapon attacks, gods add status effects and casts) so players need not hold the whole possibility space in mind.
insights.detail: Defining system boundaries helps both designers and players. Seeing a hammer on a reward door tells the player they will be offered a primary/secondary attack modification; seeing an Ares boon tells them they will get or upgrade an Ares ability, so they can plan their build in that direction.
insights.quote: it prevents the player from having to like hold in their brain the entire possibility space of everything they could possibly do to their build

insights.claim: Hades offers about nine hammer options per weapon because players see roughly two hammers per run, and picking one blocks others, leaving enough variety that consecutive runs don't repeat.
insights.detail: Content was constrained during early access. Nine was the magic number found through playtests (credited to design lead Amir): after one choice blocks some options, around six remain at the most conservative estimate, enough to keep consecutive runs with the same weapon from offering the same options.
insights.quote: we wanted to give about nine options so that on any successive run uh any consecutive run with the same weapon they wouldn't see the same options

insights.claim: Giving players too many upgrades per run (e.g. three or four hammers in Hades) makes every build blend into the same powerful sludge and erases distinctiveness.
insights.detail: Lai invokes Kate Compton's 10,000 bowls of oatmeal. With too many hammers, gun runs always ended as a triple-quintuple rocket launcher and sword runs as a massive AOE parry. A bug that let players game the reward table for four hammers produced exactly this.
insights.quote: all of the players attacks kind of like blended together into this um like powerful sludge

insights.claim: In Hades, the best combos are intentional, player-driven and not available every run, so players must improvise rather than chase one fixed build.
insights.detail: Experienced players gain some control through keepsakes that guarantee certain gods, but the designers liked that a desired combination could not simply be chased down every run, forcing improvisation, which players responded to.
insights.quote: combos that worked for us were combos that felt like really intentional really player driven and really weren't available every run

insights.claim: Hades implements boons and hammers as 'traits' that add, subtract, multiply or toggle numeric and boolean attributes in JSON-like data defining each projectile and ability.
insights.detail: Everything affecting the player is a trait. The Ares Blade Rift projectile is defined by attributes like piercing, speed, range, damage rate, impact velocity (zero means no knockback) and duration; traits modify these values to change how any ability works.
insights.quote: a bunch of numbers in JSON that formed the basis of every ability

insights.claim: Stacking trait modifiers in a system that is meant to be order-agnostic but is not produces bugs, as when a Dionysus poison fog in Hades instead detonated repeatedly with a certain shield combination.
insights.detail: Lai notes the trait system caused many bugs because the effects were supposed to be independent of application order but actually were not; the Dionysus bug arose from abilities applied in an unexpected sequence.
insights.quote: systems that um are supposed to be order agnostic but aren't actually

insights.claim: Hades uses rich mythological themes (e.g. Zeus) as a generator for parallel art and mechanics, with each god's character suggesting new abilities.
insights.detail: Thinking about what Zeus grants spins up art and ability ideas in parallel. When the Wrath (call) system was added, Zeus got abilities reflecting his vengeful mythic character; Lai describes this as a self-feeding water wheel of content.
insights.quote: having uh for example Zeus as a as an idea for a god allows us allows a lot of art to be spun up

insights.claim: As a systemic game grows, entropy wins: new effects that should work in a vacuum keep breaking existing systems, so late development must be selective about expansion.
insights.detail: Lai relays programming lead Gavin's house-of-cards analogy: build the base wide early, because everything added later builds toward the fragile top. An ability that cleared a debuff for bonus damage forced a rework of the debuff system, which never anticipated conditional clearing.
insights.quote: as you add things onto it you're always kind of building up towards uh the top of the house of cards your entropy is always going to win

insights.claim: Hades relied heavily on early access and speedrunning players to find overpowered combinations, such as a Dionysus/Athena duo that cancelled any projectile.
insights.detail: Answering how they avoided overpowered combos, Lai said they let imaginations run wild, and passionate early access and speedrunning players found design holes where things got too powerful too quickly.
insights.quote: how much the speed running and the early access community helped Hades with the development of it and just like finding design holes

insights.claim: To keep Hades' design space manageable, an ability that crosses system silos is split into separate pieces, e.g. a standalone debuff for a god boon and a secondary-attack change for a weapon or aspect.
insights.detail: Lai says no god boon may change your secondary attack and also add a debuff, because breaking the silos makes the space unmanageable; instead the idea is split so each part fits its own system.
insights.quote: it's best to split that up into something that adds uh a debuff that can stand on its own and a special secondary attack

insights.claim: Supergiant filtered brainstormed boons by both coolness and fit with Hades' fast-paced play, shelving ideas like a self-freezing invulnerability block that would self-stun the player.
insights.detail: Lai and design lead Amir rated boons on whether they would be cool and how easy and fitting they would be. A repeatedly attempted active parry system kept failing; shelved ideas are revisited later, with internal playtesting trimming things down.
insights.quote: we rated them on both like a this will be really cool

insights.claim: Supergiant ran 'boon storms': spreadsheet brainstorms listing every association with a god per ability slot, then filtered down to a strong core identity plus flourishes.
insights.detail: For Dionysus, the team listed anything from bacchanals to satyrs to wine for each modifier slot. Poseidon's core identity is knockback, but a narrative joke that he gives you stuff found in his couch became a thematic side branch giving random items.
insights.quote: we just like filter that down over time to like what we thought was a cool a really good strong core identity while retaining these like flourishes

insights.claim: Hades bounds per-run upgrade counts (about two or three hammers, at most four gods, at most two Hermes boons) to control how wide or deep a build can get and avoid screen-filling chaos.
insights.detail: These 'bumpers' combine with each system's defined role to give a predictable slice of breadth versus depth by the end of a run, reducing (not eliminating) the chaotic builds seen in other games.
insights.quote: you won't see more than like two or three hammers per game uh you won't see more than four gods per game
